nameStory: The genus name Gammarellus comes from the Latin 'gammarus,' meaning shrimp or lobster, with the diminutive ending '-ellus' meaning 'little.' So this tiny amphipod is essentially named 'little shrimp,' which perfectly captures its appearance as a miniature version of its larger crustacean cousins. The species name 'angulosus' means 'angular' or 'having angles,' referring to its somewhat pointed body segments.
description: Gammarellus angulosus is a tiny marine amphipod, essentially a microscopic shrimp-like creature that looks like a translucent comma when swimming sideways through the water. These little crustaceans are usually less than half an inch long, with compressed bodies that curve slightly like a parenthesis. They have multiple pairs of legs adapted for both swimming and crawling, and two pairs of antennae that they use to sense their watery world. You'll need to look closely or use a magnifying glass to appreciate their intricate, almost crystalline appearance.

idTips.label: Curved swimming posture
idTips.description: Swims on its side in a distinctive C-shaped curve, almost like a tiny transparent shrimp doing barrel rolls through the water

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: Body is nearly see-through with a slight pearl or glass-like quality, sometimes with a faint greenish or yellowish tint

idTips.label: Multiple leg pairs
idTips.description: Seven pairs of legs visible along the body, some paddle-like for swimming, others more claw-like for grasping

idTips.label: Two antenna pairs
idTips.description: Two distinct sets of antennae extending from the head, constantly twitching and probing the water like tiny feelers

idTips.label: Rapid jerky movements
idTips.description: Moves in quick, darting motions rather than smooth gliding, often appearing to hop through the water

habitat: Found in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools, under seaweed, and among submerged rocks during low tide. They prefer areas with good water circulation and often hide in the spaces between barnacles, mussels, and rockweed. Look for them in the intertidal zone where waves regularly splash but don't create too much turbulence.

seasonality.spring: Active in warming tide pools as marine life begins to flourish. Best spotted during calm, sunny days when the water is clear.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with highest populations visible. Most easily observed during low tide on warm days when they're actively swimming and feeding.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek deeper, more protected waters. Often found clustered under seaweed and in rock crevices.
seasonality.winter: Much less visible as they retreat to deeper waters and become less active. Occasionally found in deeper tide pools on unusually warm days.

funFact: These tiny amphipods can survive being completely dried out during extreme low tides by hiding in moist crevices, then spring back to life when the water returns—essentially playing dead for hours at a time!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small amphipods and copepods in tide pools, but Gammarellus angulosus is distinguished by its sideways swimming style and comma-shaped posture. Remember: 'G for curved like the letter G' when it swims on its side.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called amphipods, these creatures aren't actually pods at all—the name comes from Greek meaning 'different feet' because they have specialized leg types for different functions. Many people mistake them for baby shrimp, but they're fully grown adults of their own distinct crustacean group.
compareHints: **Note: Limited reference data available for this species** Since this appears to be the only Gammarellus species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other small amphipods like Gammarus species, which tend to be larger and less translucent. Gammarellus angulosus is typically smaller, more transparent, and has a more pronounced curved swimming posture than its Gammarus relatives.
